body.rationale:
Equal weight is the only method here that consumes neither return forecasts nor a covariance estimate, so no estimation error from the CMAs or the matrix enters the weights. That matters now. The regime is expansion, and the CMAs behind the return-optimized proposals are judged forecasts that carry real noise. DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal (2009) found that 1/N is hard to beat out of sample when estimation windows are short relative to the number of assets, and 18 assets is that case. The Meucci effective number of assets is 18.0 of 18, the maximum, so the portfolio is not exposed to any single forecast or any single bad covariance entry.

The ex-ante numbers are respectable without being tuned. Volatility of 8.41% sits inside the 8-12% band. Expected return is 6.71% and Sharpe 0.37. Tracking error to the IPS benchmark is 4.36%, and the portfolio passes the ex-ante return, volatility and tracking-error limits. None of this came from tuning, because the method has no parameter. The IPS is ratified, but the drawdown limit is a backtest measure the CRO checks later, so I do not claim full compliance. Most risk-only methods built without cash-like assets still land just under the 8% floor, and equal weight clears it only because it keeps the full universe, including cash, short Treasuries and the equity sleeves.

The cost of the method is that it is blind to risk. Every asset gets the same dollar weight regardless of volatility, so risk is not diversified. The equity-like sleeves (six equity funds, REITs, high yield, EM debt, commodities) make up most of the portfolio's variance, while cash and short Treasuries contribute almost nothing. The diversification is in dollars, not in risk. Risk parity, HRP and the covariance-based methods are better at spreading risk. Equal weight earns its place as the robust baseline and a hedge against forecast error, not as the risk-efficient answer.

In the CIO's ensemble I would expect it to supply a stable, high-breadth anchor that pulls the blend away from the concentration and noise of methods that rely on forecasts. The tilt vs benchmark is large in the long US-large-cap position (it is far underweight there) and the benchmark's intermediate Treasury allocation, so this portfolio carries meaningful active risk. That is the 4.36% tracking error, and it is a deliberate by-product of holding all 18 assets rather than a view.
body.notes: Key assumption: Expected returns and covariances cannot be estimated precisely enough for an optimiser to add value out of sample, so the cost of the estimation error exceeds the gain from tailoring weights to risk or return. Main weakness: It ignores risk entirely. Equal dollar weights across assets that range from about 0.6% to over 20% volatility mean the equity-like and credit sleeves dominate portfolio variance, and the cash and short Treasury weights do little work. It does not diversify risk, it holds 5.6% in cash that dilutes return in an expansion, and its 4.36% tracking error comes from the way 1/N is built (spreading across everything the benchmark ignores), not from any view. Preferred when: When the CMAs are noisy or low-conviction, when the covariance matrix is poorly conditioned or estimated from short history relative to 18 assets, and when the CIO wants a robust, transparent ensemble anchor. It is also preferred when the ex-ante volatility band must be met without a tuned parameter, since it does so here at 8.41%. Invalidated if: It is the wrong choice if the judged CMAs turn out to be reliable enough that return-optimized methods earn their Sharpe out of sample, if a risk-structured method (risk parity, HRP) delivers a clearly higher Sharpe at similar volatility, or if a regime shift (for example a late-cycle sell-off in equities, credit and commodities together) makes the 1/N overweight of risky assets produce a drawdown breach in the CRO's backtest check. A drawdown breach would also be a direct IPS failure.
